extracted.intended_audience: judges, lawyers, administrative agencies, and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for determining when courts should require clear congressional authorization for an agency action (the Major Questions Doctrine) and for interpreting Section 111 ('best system') of the Clean Air Act in that context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine applies to matters of great political or economic significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine applies when an agency seeks to resolve a question of 'great political significance' or to address a question that is 'vitally important' to the Nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court has applied the doctrine where an agency action would have effectively banned physician-assisted suicide, mandated COVID–19 vaccines nationwide (NFIB v. OSHA), or where the EPA claimed power to force plants 'to cease [operating] altogether.' When an agency seeks to resolve issues that everyone agrees are vitally important, courts look for clear congressional authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of Congress considering and rejecting similar legislation is telling
rubrics_metrics.description: When Congress has 'considered and rejected' bills authorizing something akin to the agency’s proposed course of action, that fact is suggestive that Congress did not authorize the agency to take that action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may treat failed legislation as evidence that the agency is attempting to 'work [a]round' the legislative process. The concurrence notes prior catalogues of failed legislative proposals (e.g., cataloguing failed proposals similar to the CPP) and treats those failures as relevant to whether authority was conferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulating a significant portion of the American economy or imposing billions in private spending requires clear authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must point to clear congressional authorization when it seeks to regulate 'a significant portion of the American economy' or require 'billions of dollars in spending' by private persons or entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court has held this factor applicable when agencies regulate tobacco products, eliminate rate regulation in telecommunications, subject private homes to Clean Air Act restrictions, or suspend local housing laws. Citation examples: Brown & Williamson; MCI; Utility Air; Alabama Assn. of Realtors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrusion into areas traditionally regulated by States triggers heightened scrutiny (federalism concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: The major questions doctrine often travels with the federalism clear-statement rule: courts must 'be certain of Congress's intent' before finding it legislated in areas traditionally regulated by the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an agency claims power that risks intruding on powers reserved to the States (e.g., regulation of utilities, housing), courts look for clear evidence Congress intended such a federal grant. See Gregory v. Ashcroft and Arkansas Elec. Cooperative Corp. discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine statutory provisions in the context of the overall statutory scheme; oblique language will not suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts 'must look to the legislative provisions on which the agency seeks to rely "with a view to their place in the overall statutory scheme."' Oblique or elliptical language will not supply a clear statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies cannot 'hide "elephants in mouseholes"' nor rely on 'gap filler' provisions. Examples where courts rejected agency reliance on subtle or cryptic provisions: MCI (FCC 'modify' rates), Brown & Williamson (FDA 'drugs'/'devices'), Gonzales (Attorney General and physician-assisted suicide).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the age and focus of the invoked statute relative to the problem being addressed
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unlikely that Congress would make an extraordinary grant of regulatory authority through vague language in a 'long-existant statute' focused on a different problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An old statute adopted long before the novel problem (e.g., OSHA provision adopted 40 years before the pandemic) and focused on workplace conditions rather than a societal problem is a warning sign that it does not clearly authorize a sweeping new regulation. But courts acknowledge old statutes can sometimes apply to new situations (Sedima).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency's historical interpretations and practices are relevant evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'contemporaneous' and long-held Executive Branch interpretation of a statute is entitled to some weight as evidence of the statute’s original charge to an agency; conversely, the want of prior assertion of power by those who would be alert to it is significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agency 'in its half century of existence, ha[d] never before adopted' a power it now claims, that is telling (NFIB v. OSHA example). Brown & Williamson noted FDA had for decades said it lacked power to regulate cigarettes. Courts treat 'unheralded power' claims with skepticism (Utility Air).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mismatch between challenged action and agency's mission/expertise warrants skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Skepticism may be merited when there is a mismatch between an agency’s challenged action and its congressionally assigned mission and expertise; Congress presumably would not task an agency without comparative expertise to make certain policy judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: public health agency regulating housing (Alabama Assn. of Realtors); OSHA ordaining broad public health measures (NFIB v. OSHA). The Court has rejected agency actions falling outside an agency’s traditional sphere of expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for clear evidence that Congress actually afforded the claimed power
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency seeks to resolve a major policy question, courts 'look for clear evidence that the people’s representatives in Congress have actually afforded the agency the power it claims.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concurrence emphasizes that because the EPA's approach would effectively 'resolve for itself the sort of question normally reserved for Congress,' courts require clear congressional authorization and will examine statutory text, legislative history, failed legislation, and related indicia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine is a form of clear-statement rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The major questions doctrine functions as a clear-statement rule among other judicial doctrines requiring explicit congressional authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concurrence notes the law is 'full of clear-statement rules' and treats the major questions doctrine as one such rule, comparable to federalism, mens rea, sovereign immunity presumptions, etc., used to resolve whether a statute clearly authorizes significant agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory constraints on the 'best system' under Section 111(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §7411(a)(1) EPA must determine 'the degree of emission limitation achievable through the application of the best system of emission reduction which (taking into account the cost of achieving such reduction and any nonair quality health and environmental impact and energy requirements) the [EPA] Administrator determines has been adequately demonstrated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This language directs EPA to: (1) identify a 'best system of emission reduction' that has been 'adequately demonstrated'; and (2) account for costs, nonair health/environmental impacts, and energy requirements when setting the emissions limit achievable through that system. Those constraints have led EPA historically to exclude certain measures from the "best system."

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'system' in 'best system of emission reduction' — breadth and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'system' can mean 'a set of measures that work together to reduce emissions' or a 'complex unity formed of many often diverse parts subject to a common plan or serving a common purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress's use of a broad term like 'system' grants EPA latitude to select coordinated or multi-part measures (e.g., generation shifting). A broad term is not necessarily a 'vague' one; surrounding statutory constraints (costs, nonair impacts, adequate demonstration) limit the breadth.
